note: Hand-edited source corpus for the Today in Church History layer (feature: the memory of the just). Build with `npm run history` — never hand-edit public/data/history. Every entry cites at least one public-domain source; text is drawn from those works, NOT AI-paraphrased. `verified` is false until checked against the named edition (the §3.4 ledger convention). Multiple events may share a `day` (different years); the build groups and sorts them by year.

events.title: St. Camillus de Lellis dies in Rome
events.shortBlurb: The soldier-turned-servant of the sick, founder of the Ministers of the Infirm, died in Rome — a pioneer of organized, tender care for the dying whose red cross went before the Red Cross by centuries…
body: Camillus de Lellis, a onetime soldier and gambler converted to a life of penance, founded at Rome the Order of Clerks Regular, Ministers of the Infirm (the Camillians), to serve the sick in body and soul. His followers wore a large red cross on their habits and pledged to attend the plague-stricken and the dying even at the risk of their lives.

He died in Rome on 14 July 1614. Beatified in 1742 and canonized in 1746, he was later named, with St. John of God, patron of the sick and of hospitals, and patron of nurses and of the Red Cross tradition of mercy to the wounded.

events.title: Keble’s “National Apostasy” sermon begins the Oxford Movement
events.shortBlurb: John Keble mounted the pulpit of the University Church at Oxford and preached against the State’s meddling in the Church — the sermon John Henry Newman would later date as the true start of the movement that led many toward Rome…
body: On 14 July 1833 John Keble preached the Assize Sermon, “National Apostasy,” at St. Mary’s, the University Church of Oxford, protesting the British government’s suppression of Irish bishoprics as an intrusion upon the divine constitution of the Church.

John Henry Newman afterward reckoned this sermon the beginning of the Oxford Movement, which sought to recover the Catholic heritage of the English Church. Its studies of antiquity led Newman and many others, over the following years, into full communion with the Catholic Church.

events.title: The First Crusade captures Jerusalem
events.shortBlurb: After a long march and siege, the armies of the First Crusade breached the walls and took the Holy City, ending the expedition summoned four years earlier at Clermont…
body: On 15 July 1099 the soldiers of the First Crusade, after a siege of some weeks, stormed the walls and captured Jerusalem, the goal of the expedition preached by Pope Urban II at Clermont in 1095. A Latin kingdom of Jerusalem was set up in the aftermath.
The capture was marked by great slaughter of the city’s inhabitants, a violence later generations remembered with sorrow. The crusader hold on Jerusalem lasted until Saladin retook it in 1187.

events.title: The First Council of Nicaea opens
events.shortBlurb: The first ecumenical council of the Church gathered at Nicaea under the Emperor Constantine to answer the Arian denial of Christ’s divinity, and gave the Church its Creed…
body: In 325 some three hundred bishops assembled at Nicaea in Asia Minor for the first ecumenical council, convened to settle the crisis raised by Arius, who taught that the Son was a creature and not truly God. Against him the council professed the Son “consubstantial (homoousios) with the Father.”

From this council comes the heart of the Nicene Creed still professed at Mass, together with a common rule for computing the date of Easter. It stands as the pattern of the Church’s conciliar teaching.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “The First Council of Nicaea”

events.title: Urban II preaches the First Crusade at Clermont
events.shortBlurb: At the Council of Clermont Pope Urban II called Christendom to aid the Eastern churches and free the holy places, and the crowd is said to have answered, “Deus vult” — God wills it…
body: At the close of the Council of Clermont in France, on 27 November 1095, Pope Urban II preached to a great throng, urging the knights of the West to cease their private wars and go to the aid of the Christians of the East and the holy places of Jerusalem.
The response, tradition records, was the cry “Deus vult” — God wills it — and the taking of the cross. So began the First Crusade, which reached Jerusalem in 1099.

events.title: Pope Leo III crowns Charlemagne Emperor
events.shortBlurb: On Christmas Day in St. Peter’s, Pope Leo III set a crown on the head of the Frankish king Charlemagne and hailed him Emperor, binding the fortunes of the Papacy and the West…
body: During Mass on Christmas Day of the year 800, in the basilica of St. Peter at Rome, Pope Leo III crowned Charles the Great, king of the Franks, as Emperor of the Romans, and the people acclaimed him.

The event marked the rise of a Christian empire in the West and set the pattern of relations between the Papacy and the emperors for centuries — a partnership, and often a struggle, at the heart of medieval Christendom.

events.title: Pius IX defines the Immaculate Conception
events.shortBlurb: In the bull Ineffabilis Deus, Pope Pius IX solemnly defined that the Blessed Virgin Mary was preserved free from original sin from the first moment of her conception…
body: On 8 December 1854, in the Apostolic Constitution Ineffabilis Deus, Pope Pius IX defined as a dogma of faith that the Blessed Virgin Mary, in the first instant of her conception, was by a singular grace of God and in view of the merits of Christ preserved free from all stain of original sin.
Four years later the apparitions at Lourdes, in which the Lady named herself “the Immaculate Conception,” were widely received as a confirmation of the definition.

events.title: Luther posts the Ninety-Five Theses
events.shortBlurb: At Wittenberg an Augustinian friar named Martin Luther set out ninety-five theses against the preaching of indulgences — the spark, by long tradition, of the Protestant Reformation…
body: On 31 October 1517 Martin Luther, an Augustinian friar and professor at Wittenberg, published ninety-five theses disputing the preaching of indulgences. What began as an academic protest widened rapidly into a break with the Church that divided Western Christendom.
In answer the Church undertook the reform and definition of doctrine at the Council of Trent (1545–1563), the great work of the Catholic Reformation.

events.title: The Edict of Milan grants toleration to Christians
events.shortBlurb: The emperors Constantine and Licinius agreed to grant Christians freedom of worship, ending the age of persecution in the Roman Empire…
body: In 313 the emperors Constantine and Licinius met at Milan and agreed on a policy of religious toleration, restoring to Christians the freedom to worship and the property that had been seized in the persecutions. Though not itself a formal single decree in the later sense, the agreement — known as the Edict of Milan — marked the decisive turn from persecution to peace for the Church in the Roman world.
Within a few generations Christianity would pass from a persecuted sect to the faith of the Empire.

events.title: The Council of Nicaea proclaims the Creed
events.shortBlurb: The first ecumenical council, gathered against Arianism, confessed the Son to be “consubstantial” with the Father…
body: The bishops assembled at Nicaea in 325, the first ecumenical council, met to answer the teaching of Arius that the Son was a creature. Against it they confessed the Son to be “consubstantial” (homoousios) with the Father, true God of true God, and set down the Creed that, with later additions, the Church still professes.
The council also fixed a common method for calculating the date of Easter.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), General Church history

events.title: Death of Pope St. Gregory VII
events.shortBlurb: The reforming pope of the Investiture Controversy, who brought the emperor to penance at Canossa, died in exile at Salerno…
body: Gregory VII (Hildebrand) was the great reforming pope who fought simony and the lay investiture of bishops, and who in 1077 brought the Emperor Henry IV to do penance in the snow at Canossa. Driven at last from Rome, he died in exile at Salerno in 1085 with the words, “I have loved justice and hated iniquity; therefore I die in exile.”
His reform reshaped the medieval Church's independence from secular power.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 25 May

events.title: The fall of Constantinople
events.shortBlurb: The ancient Christian capital of the East fell to the Ottoman Turks, ending the Byzantine Empire after a thousand years…
body: On 29 May 1453 the city of Constantinople, capital of the Christian East for over a thousand years, fell to the army of the Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II after a long siege. The great church of Hagia Sophia was turned to other use, and the Byzantine Empire came to its end.
The event sent Greek scholars and manuscripts westward and pressed hard upon Christian Europe for generations.

sources.text: Gibbon, Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire (public domain)

events.title: The victory of Lepanto
events.shortBlurb: A Christian fleet of the Holy League turned back the Ottoman navy in the Gulf of Corinth; the day gave rise to the feast of the Rosary…
body: On 7 October 1571 the fleet of the Holy League, gathered by Pope St. Pius V, met and defeated the Ottoman navy in the Gulf of Lepanto, checking Turkish power in the Mediterranean. The pope attributed the victory to the intercession of Our Lady, invoked through the Rosary by the faithful of Rome.
In thanksgiving he established the commemoration kept today as the feast of Our Lady of the Rosary.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “Feast of the Holy Rosary”

events.title: The Council of Trent opens
events.shortBlurb: The great council of the Catholic Reformation began its work, defining doctrine and reforming discipline for centuries to come…
body: The Council of Trent opened on 13 December 1545 and, meeting in sessions over eighteen years, answered the doctrinal challenges of the Reformation and undertook a thorough reform of Church discipline. It clarified the teaching on Scripture and tradition, justification, the sacraments, and the Mass, and set in motion the seminaries and catechesis of the Catholic Reformation.
Its decrees shaped Catholic life until the twentieth century.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), General Church history

events.title: The death of St. Francis of Assisi
events.shortBlurb: The Poverello died at the Portiuncula near Assisi; his passing is kept by the Franciscans as the Transitus…
body: On the evening of 3 October 1226 St. Francis of Assisi died at the little church of the Portiuncula, having asked to be laid on the bare ground and having added a final stanza to his Canticle of the Creatures welcoming “Sister Death.” His passing is commemorated by the Franciscan family as the Transitus, the eve of his feast.
Two years later he was canonized by Pope Gregory IX.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 4 October
